extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate mathematics students (introductory set theory / discrete math)
extracted.subtask_description: Principles, theorems, and constructive techniques for comparing cardinalities of sets (finite, countably infinite, uncountable), including diagonal arguments, injective/surjective/bijective constructions, and the Cantor–Bernstein theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor's theorem (|A| < |P(A)|)
rubrics_metrics.description: There exists an injection A → P(A) but no surjection A → P(A); hence |A| < |P(A)|.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Define B = { x ∈ A : x ∉ f(x) } for a purported surjection f : A → P(A). Since B ∈ P(A), surjectivity gives a ∈ A with f(a)=B; considering whether a ∈ B or a ∉ B yields a contradiction in either case (diagonal argument). This proves no surjection A → P(A) exists while the map a ↦ {a} shows an injection A → P(A). Use this to conclude strict inequality of cardinalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterated power-set yields strictly increasing cardinalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Applying Cantor's theorem repeatedly to a set (e.g., N) gives an infinite ascending chain of distinct infinite cardinalities: ℵ0 = |N| < |P(N)| < |P(P(N))| < ···.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start with a countably infinite set (like N) and apply the power set operation repeatedly; each step strictly increases cardinality by Cantor's theorem. Use this to argue there are many different 'sizes' of infinity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 13.8: infinite subset of a countably infinite set is countably infinite
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is an infinite subset of a countably infinite set B, then A is countably infinite.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List B as b1, b2, b3, ... and form a list of A by scanning that list and selecting members that lie in A; since A is infinite this produces an infinite list. This is a standard method to prove a subset of a countable set is countable when infinite.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 13.9: uncountable subset forces superset uncountable
rubrics_metrics.description: If U ⊆ A and U is uncountable, then A is uncountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof by contradiction: if A were countably infinite then (by Theorem 13.8) U, an infinite subset of A, would be countably infinite—contradiction. Use this to deduce uncountability of ambient sets from known uncountable subsets (e.g., deducing R^2 is uncountable from a copy of R inside it).

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion for |A| ≤ |B| and technique using injections
rubrics_metrics.description: |A| ≤ |B| means there is an injection A → B (equivalently |A| < |B| or |A| = |B|).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To show one cardinality is at most another, it suffices to construct an injective map. This viewpoint underlies many cardinality comparisons and reduces problems of equating or comparing sizes to finding injections/surjections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor–Bernstein–Schröder theorem (Theorem 13.10)
rubrics_metrics.description: If |A| ≤ |B| and |B| ≤ |A| (equivalently there are injections f : A → B and g : B → A), then |A| = |B|; i.e., there exists a bijection h : A → B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructively partition A into G = ⋃_{k≥0} (g◦f)^k(A − g(B)) and W = A − G. Define h(x)=f(x) for x∈G and h(x)=g^{-1}(x) for x∈W (g^{-1} defined on g(B)). Prove h is injective by case analysis (both in G, both in W, or one in each) and surjective by considering g(b)∈A for b∈B and whether g(b)∈W or G. This theorem means to prove two sets have same cardinality it often suffices to give injections in both directions rather than an explicit bijection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Using Cantor–Bernstein to equate seemingly different sets (examples)
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples: [0,1) and (0,1) have equal cardinality; more generally bijections can be guaranteed when injections both ways are known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide injections in each direction (e.g., f(x)=2x injects [0,1)→(0,1) and g(x)=x is injection (0,1)→[0,1)) and apply Cantor–Bernstein to obtain a bijection. This demonstrates how CBS simplifies constructing bijections that would otherwise be tricky.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 13.11: |R| = |P(N)| (cardinality of continuum equals power set of naturals)
rubrics_metrics.description: The real numbers (or equivalently the interval [0,1) or (0,1)) have the same cardinality as P(N).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exhibit injections both ways and apply Cantor–Bernstein. Example constructions: f : [0,1) → P(N) maps a decimal 0.b1b2b3... to the set {10^{b1}, 10^{2 b2}, 10^{3 b3}, ...} (ensure unique decimal representation by disallowing tail of repeating 9s); g : P(N) → [0,1) maps X to the binary-like decimal 0.b1b2b3... with bi=1 if i∈X else 0. Show both maps are injective and apply Cantor–Bernstein to get a bijection and thus equality of cardinalities. Note the need to handle uniqueness issues in decimal expansions (exclude terminating with infinite 9s) when defining injective decimal-based maps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical proof strategies for cardinality statements (exercises and suggestions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Typical strategies: construct injections or surjections, use diagonal arguments to rule out surjections (as in Cantor), apply Cantor–Bernstein when injections both ways are available, and compare via known sets (e.g., embed copies of R in R^2 or N into product spaces).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercises illustrate these techniques: prove complex numbers uncountable by embedding R×R, show |R^2|=|R| by explicit pairing or interleaving digits, prove |P(N×N)| = |P(N)|, and use injections+surjections to infer equalities/inequalities of cardinalities. When proving 'uncountable' often demonstrate an uncountable subset or use diagonalization; when proving 'countable' give an explicit listing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/contextual constraints: continuum hypothesis and independence
rubrics_metrics.description: The continuum hypothesis (no cardinalities strictly between ℵ0 and |R|) is independent of the standard Zermelo–Fraenkel axioms: Gödel and Cohen showed it can neither be proved nor disproved from those axioms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understand that certain cardinality assertions (like the continuum hypothesis) are undecidable within standard set theory, so whether one accepts them is a matter of adopting additional axioms or remaining agnostic; most mainstream mathematics is unaffected by this choice. This contextual information helps frame limits of provability in cardinality questions.
